title: Glomerular Diseases and Renal Failure
subject: Renal and Urinary System (RENL)

overview.intro: This chapter explains how injury to the glomerular filtration barrier produces the two classic clinical patterns, nephritic and nephrotic syndrome, and how biopsy findings, complement levels, and urine sediment identify the specific disease. It then follows glomerular and tubular injury to its end points, acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease. Board questions give a urinalysis, a set of labs, or a biopsy description and ask you to name the lesion, its cause, or its complication. If you can place an immune deposit on the filter and predict what that location does to inflammation, protein loss, and filtration, most of these questions become reasoning rather than recall.
prerequisites: Structure of the glomerular filtration barrier: fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, podocytes, and mesangium (UR-2, UR-3)
Determinants of glomerular filtration rate and Starling forces across glomerular and systemic capillaries
Complement activation by the classical, lectin, and alternative pathways
Type II and type III hypersensitivity and immune complex deposition
Tubular handling of sodium, potassium, urea, and acid

connections.how: Glomerular pressure, tubuloglomerular feedback, and tubular sodium handling explain hyperfiltration, prerenal indices, and the volume and electrolyte disturbances of renal failure.
Most glomerulonephritis is antibody mediated, and the complement pathway each disease activates predicts whether serum C3 and C4 fall.
Group A streptococci, hepatitis B and C, and HIV cause specific glomerular lesions, while pyelonephritis is recognized in the same sediment by WBC casts.
Diabetes and hypertension are the leading causes of chronic kidney disease, and kidney failure in turn worsens hypertension, heart failure, and bone mineral balance.
Plasma cell dyscrasias cause AL amyloid, nephrotic syndrome causes hypercoagulability, and chronic kidney disease causes anemia and platelet dysfunction.

blocks.text: The glomerular filtration barrier has three layers. Fenestrated endothelium faces the blood, the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) of type IV collagen, laminin, and negatively charged heparan sulfate sits in the middle, and podocyte foot processes joined by slit diaphragms (built from nephrin and podocin) face Bowman space. Together they restrict filtration by size and charge, so normal urine contains less than about 150 mg of protein per day and less than 30 mg of albumin. Glomerular diseases present in two broad patterns that depend on which part of the barrier is injured and whether inflammation is present.

Nephritic syndrome is inflammatory. Immune deposits in the mesangium or on the blood side of the GBM activate complement, and C5a and Fc receptor binding recruit neutrophils and monocytes. Proliferating glomerular cells and leukocytes crowd the capillary lumens, which reduces the filtering surface and lowers GFR, so blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine rise and urine output falls. Breaks in the inflamed capillary wall let red cells into the urine, where they are molded into RBC casts. Because the tubules are intact and keep reabsorbing sodium while filtration falls, salt and water are retained, producing hypertension and edema. Protein leaks through the damaged wall, but the low GFR keeps the total usually below 3.5 g/day.

Nephrotic syndrome is a failure of the protein barrier with little inflammation. Podocyte injury or deposits on the urinary side of the GBM disrupt the slit diaphragms, and proteinuria exceeds 3.5 g/day in adults (in children, above about 40 mg/m2 per hour). Serum albumin falls below about 3 g/dL (reference about 3.5 to 5.0 g/dL), and edema, hyperlipidemia, and lipiduria with fatty casts follow. Hematuria is slight and GFR is often normal at first.

Deposit location is the most useful rule. Mesangial and subendothelial deposits are exposed to circulating leukocytes and complement, so they cause nephritic disease; subepithelial deposits are separated from the blood by the GBM, so complement injures the podocyte without a leukocyte influx and the result is nephrotic. Some diseases, notably lupus nephritis and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, produce a mixed nephritic and nephrotic picture.

blocks.predict: Why does a child with acute glomerulonephritis become hypertensive even though the problem is in the glomerulus, not the vessels?
blocks.explain: Inflammation lowers GFR, but the tubules still reabsorb sodium avidly, so filtered sodium falls further than intake. The positive sodium balance expands extracellular volume, which raises blood pressure and causes edema.

sections.title: Urine sediment as a map of the nephron

blocks.text: Casts form when uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall protein), secreted by the thick ascending limb, gels in the distal tubule and collecting duct. Low flow, concentrated urine, and an acidic pH favor gelling. Anything trapped in the matrix was in the tubule lumen when the cast formed, so a cellular cast proves that the cells came from the kidney rather than from the bladder or urethra. Hyaline casts contain matrix alone and are nonspecific: they appear in concentrated urine, after exercise, and in prerenal states.

Red cells localize bleeding. Glomerular red cells are dysmorphic, with blebs and irregular outlines (acanthocytes), because they are squeezed through breaks in the GBM and then exposed to changing osmolality and pH along the tubule. RBC casts are specific for glomerular bleeding. Uniform (isomorphic) red cells without casts point to the collecting system, ureter, or bladder, as with stones, tumors, or cystitis. A dipstick positive for heme with no red cells on microscopy suggests myoglobin from rhabdomyolysis or free hemoglobin from hemolysis.

WBC casts mean leukocytes entered the tubules, which happens in tubulointerstitial inflammation: acute pyelonephritis, with bacteriuria and fever, and acute interstitial nephritis, often a drug hypersensitivity with eosinophils. Necrotic tubular cells slough into the lumen in acute tubular necrosis (ATN) and break down into the coarse muddy brown granular casts of that disease. Fatty casts and oval fat bodies are tubular cells and casts loaded with filtered lipoproteins, showing a Maltese cross under polarized light. Waxy casts are casts that degenerated during prolonged stasis in dilated, low-flow tubules, so broad waxy casts indicate advanced chronic kidney disease.

blocks.title: Urinary casts and what they localize

blocks.caption: A cast places its contents inside the tubule, so the sediment identifies which compartment of the kidney is injured.

blocks.text: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is the prototype of immune complex (type III hypersensitivity) nephritic disease. It follows infection with nephritogenic strains of group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes, and it is most common in children between about 5 and 12 years old. The latent period is about 1 to 3 weeks after pharyngitis and about 3 to 6 weeks after impetigo. This delay is the time needed to make antibody against streptococcal antigens, so the kidney becomes involved after the infection has resolved.

The main nephritogenic antigens are streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B (SpeB) and a nephritis-associated plasmin receptor. They lodge in the glomerulus or circulate as immune complexes, and complement is activated mainly by the alternative pathway. Serum C3 therefore falls while C4 is usually normal, and C3 returns to normal within about 8 weeks. A low C3 that persists beyond that suggests another disease, such as membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis or lupus.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis
steps: Pharyngitis or impetigo with a nephritogenic group A strain
Antibodies form over 1 to 6 weeks
Antigen-antibody complexes deposit in glomeruli
Complement activation, mainly alternative pathway; serum C3 falls
Neutrophils and monocytes infiltrate; glomerular cells proliferate
GFR falls; hematuria, oliguria, sodium retention
blocks.caption: The latent period reflects antibody production, which separates PSGN from disease caused directly by infection.

blocks.text: Light microscopy shows enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli packed with neutrophils and monocytes, a diffuse proliferative and exudative pattern. Immunofluorescence shows granular (lumpy-bumpy) IgG and C3 along capillary walls and in the mesangium. Electron microscopy shows large subepithelial humps, the distinctive finding, along with smaller subendothelial and mesangial deposits. The clinical picture follows the nephritic mechanism: cola-colored urine from hemoglobin altered in acidic urine, periorbital edema where loose tissue lets fluid collect, hypertension, and oliguria.

Evidence of recent infection supports the diagnosis. Antistreptolysin O titers rise after pharyngitis, while anti-DNase B is more reliable after skin infection because streptolysin O is inactivated by skin lipids. Most children recover completely; adults more often develop persistent disease or rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Unlike acute rheumatic fever, which follows only pharyngitis, PSGN can follow either throat or skin infection.

sections.title: IgA nephropathy and how it differs from PSGN

blocks.text: IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide. Its basis is a defect in O-glycosylation of the IgA1 hinge region, which produces galactose-deficient IgA1. IgG and IgA autoantibodies recognize the exposed hinge, and the resulting complexes deposit in the mesangium. There they stimulate mesangial cell proliferation and matrix production and activate complement through the alternative and lectin pathways. Because activation is local rather than systemic, serum C3 stays normal.

Mucosal infections of the upper respiratory or gastrointestinal tract increase production of the abnormal IgA. Because the antibodies and complexes already circulate, more deposition occurs almost at once, so episodes of gross hematuria appear within about 1 to 2 days of the infection (synpharyngitic hematuria) rather than after weeks. Between episodes, microscopic hematuria and mild proteinuria often persist. Liver disease and celiac disease are secondary associations because they impair IgA clearance or increase mucosal IgA production. IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) produces the same mesangial lesion together with palpable purpura, arthralgia, and abdominal pain.

The disease is often slowly progressive, and a minority of patients reach end-stage kidney disease over about two decades. Biopsy shows mesangial proliferation on light microscopy, dominant mesangial IgA with C3 on immunofluorescence, and mesangial deposits on electron microscopy.

blocks.title: IgA nephropathy versus poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis
rows: Abnormal IgA and antibodies already circulate
Granular IgG and C3 in capillary walls
blocks.caption: Timing and complement level are the two quickest discriminators.

blocks.title: Two patients with cola-colored urine
blocks.text: A 22-year-old man has dark urine 2 days after a sore throat; C3 is normal, and he had a similar episode last year. A 7-year-old boy has dark urine, periorbital edema, and blood pressure of 135/90 mm Hg about 3 weeks after impetigo; C3 is low. In the man, the short interval means the injurious antibody already existed, and the normal C3 means complement was not consumed systemically, which fits IgA nephropathy with mesangial IgA. In the boy, the delay matches the time to form new antibody, and the low C3 reflects alternative pathway consumption by immune complexes, which fits PSGN; anti-DNase B is the better test after skin infection, and subepithelial humps would be expected on electron microscopy.

Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) is a clinical syndrome of nephritic disease with loss of renal function over days to weeks. Its morphologic correlate is crescents in most glomeruli, often defined as more than half. RPGN is not one disease; it is the common end result of any injury severe enough to rupture glomerular capillary walls.

blocks.title: How a crescent forms
steps: Severe injury ruptures the glomerular capillary wall
Plasma proteins and fibrin leak into Bowman space
Fibrin and cytokines stimulate parietal epithelial cells
Parietal cells proliferate; monocytes and macrophages enter
Crescent compresses the tuft and blocks filtration
Untreated crescents fibrose; nephron loss is permanent
blocks.caption: Cellular crescents become fibrocellular and then fibrous, which is why RPGN can cause irreversible renal failure within weeks.

blocks.text: Immunofluorescence separates three types by the pattern of immunoglobulin along the GBM. In type I, anti-GBM disease, autoantibodies bind the noncollagenous (NC1) domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen. The antigen is spread evenly along the membrane, so IgG and C3 appear as a smooth linear stain. The same antigen is present in alveolar basement membrane, so pulmonary hemorrhage with hemoptysis may accompany the nephritis (Goodpasture syndrome); smoking and inhaled hydrocarbons that expose the lung antigen are recognized triggers.

In type II, immune complex RPGN, deposits are discrete and the stain is granular. Any immune complex nephritis can become crescentic, including PSGN, lupus nephritis, IgA nephropathy, and IgA vasculitis. In type III, pauci-immune RPGN, little or no immunoglobulin is found. Most cases are renal involvement by antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) small-vessel vasculitis. Cytokines prime neutrophils to express proteinase 3 (PR3) or myeloperoxidase (MPO) on their surface; ANCA binding then activates them to degranulate and release reactive oxygen species against the glomerular endothelium, causing necrotizing lesions without immune deposits.

blocks.title: Immunofluorescence classification of RPGN
rows: Antibody to alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (PR3-ANCA, c-ANCA); microscopic polyangiitis (MPO-ANCA, p-ANCA); eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (MPO-ANCA in some)
blocks.caption: The immunofluorescence pattern reflects the antigen: continuous membrane antigen gives a linear stain, discrete complexes give a granular one, and neutrophil-mediated injury leaves little immunoglobulin.

blocks.text: Renal involvement is one of the most important determinants of outcome in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Antibodies against double-stranded DNA and nucleosomes form immune complexes that deposit in the glomerulus or form there in situ, and they activate complement by the classical pathway. Immunofluorescence typically shows a full house pattern of IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C1q. Where the deposits sit decides the clinical picture, which is why lupus can be nephritic, nephrotic, or both.

Diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis (ISN/RPS class IV) is the most common class on biopsy and the most severe. Large subendothelial deposits thicken capillary walls into rigid wire loops visible on light microscopy, and because they face the blood they recruit leukocytes and drive proliferation in at least half of the glomeruli. Patients have hematuria with RBC casts, hypertension, a falling GFR, and often heavy proteinuria; crescents may develop. Membranous lupus nephritis (class V) has subepithelial deposits, which injure podocytes without inflammation and produce nephrotic syndrome, much like primary membranous nephropathy. Classes can coexist and can change over time.

blocks.title: ISN/RPS classes of lupus nephritis
rows: Advanced sclerosing (90 percent or more sclerosed)
blocks.caption: Classes III and IV are proliferative and nephritic; class V is nephrotic.

blocks.text: Serology tracks the mechanism. Antinuclear antibody is sensitive but not specific. Anti-dsDNA is highly specific for SLE, and its titer tends to rise with active nephritis because these antibodies form the complexes that injure the glomerulus. Classical pathway activation consumes both C3 and C4, so low complement with rising anti-dsDNA points to an active renal flare. Anti-Smith antibody is also specific for SLE but does not track activity. A low C4 helps separate lupus from PSGN, where C4 is usually normal.

Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) is a pattern of injury rather than a single disease. Glomeruli are hypercellular and lobular. Mesangial cells and leukocytes extend into the capillary wall between the endothelium and the GBM (mesangial interposition), and the endothelium lays down a new layer of basement membrane inside the original one. Silver or PAS stains then show a double contour, the tram-track appearance. Because the injury is both proliferative and damages the barrier, MPGN may present as nephritic syndrome, nephrotic syndrome, or a mix, and it tends to progress slowly to renal failure.

Current classification uses immunofluorescence. In immune complex MPGN, immunoglobulin and C3 deposit together, mainly in subendothelial and mesangial sites, after chronic antigen exposure. Hepatitis C, often with mixed cryoglobulinemia, is the classic cause, and hepatitis B, chronic bacterial infections such as endocarditis, autoimmune disease, and monoclonal gammopathies are others. These complexes activate the classical pathway, so C3 and often C4 are low. This group largely corresponds to the older type I.

In C3 glomerulopathy, C3 deposits with little or no immunoglobulin because the alternative pathway is uncontrolled. Dense deposit disease (formerly type II MPGN) is the best-known form, with ribbon-like, very dense deposits within the lamina densa of the GBM. Most patients have C3 nephritic factor, an IgG autoantibody that binds the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb) and protects it from inactivation by factor H. The convertase then cleaves C3 continuously, so serum C3 is very low while C4 is normal. Genetic defects in factor H produce the same effect, and dense deposit disease is associated with partial lipodystrophy.

blocks.caption: Both share mesangial interposition and tram-track basement membrane duplication.

blocks.text: Diabetic nephropathy is the leading cause of end-stage kidney disease in developed countries, and it arises from hemodynamic and metabolic injury acting together. Early in diabetes, filtered glucose increases proximal sodium and glucose cotransport, so less sodium chloride reaches the macula densa. Tubuloglomerular feedback reads this as low flow and dilates the afferent arteriole, while angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole. Glomerular capillary pressure and GFR rise above normal (hyperfiltration), and the kidneys enlarge.

The metabolic arm is nonenzymatic glycation. Glucose binds proteins without enzymes and forms advanced glycation end products that cross-link collagen, stimulate matrix synthesis through TGF-beta, and trap plasma proteins. GBM thickening, detectable by electron microscopy within a few years of onset, is the earliest structural change. Hyaline arteriolosclerosis affects both the afferent and the efferent arteriole; efferent involvement is characteristic of diabetes and keeps glomerular pressure high. Mesangial matrix expands first diffusely and then forms round, PAS-positive nodules at the periphery of the tuft, the Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesion of nodular glomerulosclerosis.

blocks.title: Progression of diabetic nephropathy
steps: Hyperglycemia raises proximal sodium and glucose reabsorption
Afferent dilation and efferent constriction cause hyperfiltration
Glycation end products thicken the GBM and expand mesangium
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis of afferent and efferent arterioles
Moderately increased albuminuria, 30 to 300 mg/day
Overt then nephrotic-range proteinuria; Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules
Glomerulosclerosis, falling GFR, end-stage kidney disease
blocks.caption: Hemodynamic stress and matrix accumulation reinforce each other; albuminuria is the first clinical sign.

blocks.text: Clinically, the first sign is moderately increased albuminuria (30 to 300 mg/day, traditionally called microalbuminuria), which a standard dipstick does not detect. Proteinuria then becomes overt and often reaches the nephrotic range, hypertension develops, and GFR declines after the period of hyperfiltration. The role of glomerular pressure is confirmed by the observation that blocking angiotensin II formation or action dilates the efferent arteriole, lowers glomerular pressure, and reduces albuminuria. Diabetes also predisposes to pyelonephritis and renal papillary necrosis, which add tubulointerstitial injury. Unlike most causes of chronic kidney disease, diabetic kidneys are often normal or large in size even when function is poor.

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is sclerosis of part of the tuft (segmental) in some glomeruli (focal). Juxtamedullary glomeruli are often affected first, so a small biopsy that samples only superficial cortex can miss the lesion. Its root cause is podocyte injury. Podocytes are terminally differentiated cells with very limited ability to replace themselves, so when they are lost, bare segments of GBM adhere to Bowman capsule, and those segments collapse and scar. Immunofluorescence is usually negative apart from nonspecific trapping of IgM and C3 in scarred areas, and electron microscopy shows foot process effacement.

Primary FSGS is thought to involve a circulating factor that injures podocytes. Genetic forms involve slit diaphragm and podocyte cytoskeletal proteins such as nephrin and podocin, and APOL1 risk variants, common in people of West African ancestry, help explain why FSGS is a leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in Black adults. Compared with minimal change disease, proteinuria is less selective, hematuria and hypertension are more common, response to corticosteroids is poor, and many patients progress to renal failure.

Secondary FSGS has several mechanisms. Obesity, sickle cell disease (with anemia-driven hyperfiltration), and loss of nephron mass overload the remaining glomeruli, as shown in the cycle below. Heroin use, especially in the past, is associated with FSGS, although adulterants may be responsible. HIV causes the collapsing variant, HIV-associated nephropathy, in which HIV infects podocytes and tubular cells and viral gene products make podocytes dedifferentiate and proliferate while the capillary tuft collapses. Tubules dilate into microcysts filled with casts, endothelial cells show tubuloreticular inclusions, the kidneys are large and echogenic, and heavy proteinuria progresses rapidly to end-stage disease. APOL1 variants also raise this risk.

steps: Nephrons are lost or demand rises (obesity, sickle cell)
Remaining glomeruli hyperfilter at high pressure
Podocytes stretch, detach, and are not replaced
Bare basement membrane adheres to Bowman capsule and scars
More nephrons are lost, increasing load on the rest
blocks.caption: This adaptive mechanism explains secondary FSGS and the steady progression of many chronic kidney diseases once nephron mass falls.

blocks.text: The complications of nephrotic syndrome follow from what the urine loses and how the liver responds. Edema has two components. Low albumin lowers plasma oncotic pressure, so fluid moves into the interstitium by Starling forces (underfill). In many patients the kidney also retains sodium directly, partly because filtered plasminogen is converted to plasmin, which cleaves and activates epithelial sodium channels in the collecting duct (overfill). The relative weight of these two mechanisms varies, and it explains why some nephrotic patients have normal or high plasma volume.

Hyperlipidemia arises because the liver responds to low oncotic pressure by increasing synthesis of lipoproteins, including apolipoprotein B-containing VLDL and LDL, while catabolism falls because lipoprotein lipase activity is reduced. Filtered lipid appears as oval fat bodies and fatty casts. Hypercoagulability comes from urinary loss of antithrombin III, a small protein that crosses the damaged filter, combined with increased hepatic synthesis of fibrinogen and other clotting factors and platelet hyperaggregability. Renal vein thrombosis is the classic result, most often in membranous nephropathy, and pulmonary embolism and deep vein thrombosis also occur.

Infection risk rises because IgG and complement factors such as factor B are lost in the urine, weakening opsonization of encapsulated bacteria. Children with nephrotic syndrome are therefore prone to Streptococcus pneumoniae peritonitis in ascitic fluid. Other carrier proteins are lost as well, including vitamin D-binding protein, thyroxine-binding globulin, and transferrin, which alters measured total hormone and iron levels.

Renal vein thrombosis presents with flank pain, hematuria, and a sudden increase in proteinuria. In men, a new left-sided varicocele may appear because the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein.

blocks.title: Mechanisms of nephrotic complications
rows: Low oncotic pressure plus primary renal sodium retention
More hepatic lipoprotein synthesis, less lipoprotein lipase activity
High LDL and cholesterol; lipiduria, fatty casts
Urinary antithrombin III loss; more hepatic clotting factors
Renal vein thrombosis, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism
Urinary loss of IgG and factor B
Loss of vitamin D-binding protein, thyroxine-binding globulin, transferrin
blocks.caption: Each complication is either a urinary loss or a hepatic response to that loss.

blocks.predict: If the liver increases synthesis of many proteins in nephrotic syndrome, why does serum albumin stay low while cholesterol rises?
blocks.explain: Albumin is small enough to be lost in the urine nearly as fast as it is made, while large lipoproteins such as LDL are too big to cross even a damaged filter, so they accumulate. Reduced lipoprotein lipase activity adds to the rise.

blocks.text: Minimal change disease (MCD) is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in young children, with a peak at about 2 to 6 years of age. Its name describes the biopsy. Light microscopy shows normal glomeruli, immunofluorescence shows no immune deposits, and only electron microscopy reveals the lesion: diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes. Proximal tubular cells may contain reabsorbed lipid, which gave the disease its older name, lipoid nephrosis.

The cause is podocyte dysfunction without immune complex deposition. A circulating factor, linked to abnormal T-cell function, is thought to alter the podocyte and its slit diaphragm, and antibodies against nephrin have been reported in some patients. The classic teaching is that loss of the negatively charged polyanions of the filter removes charge selectivity, so the small, negatively charged albumin crosses while larger proteins such as IgG are largely held back. This selective albuminuria is typical of MCD and contrasts with the nonselective proteinuria of FSGS and other structural lesions.

Because the podocytes are functionally altered rather than destroyed, the lesion is reversible. More than about 90 percent of children have complete remission of proteinuria with corticosteroids, and this response is itself a diagnostic feature that supports the immune basis of the disease. Hematuria, hypertension, and reduced GFR are uncommon, and progression to renal failure is rare. Relapses are common, however.

Secondary MCD is recognized in adults. The classic association is Hodgkin lymphoma, presumably through cytokines produced by the tumor and its reactive T cells, and nephrotic syndrome may resolve when the lymphoma is controlled. NSAIDs can cause MCD together with acute interstitial nephritis, and allergies and infections have been linked to relapses. When an adult presents with nephrotic syndrome and a biopsy shows only foot process effacement, these causes should be considered, and FSGS should be kept in mind because a small biopsy can miss segmental scars.

Membranous nephropathy is a major cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, usually after age 40. In primary disease, IgG autoantibodies, mostly of the IgG4 subclass, bind phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R), a protein on the podocyte surface. About 70 to 80 percent of primary cases have anti-PLA2R antibodies, and a smaller group has antibodies to thrombospondin type-1 domain-containing 7A. The complexes form in situ beneath the podocyte, producing subepithelial deposits.

Because the deposits sit on the urinary side of the GBM, circulating leukocytes cannot reach them, and the disease is not inflammatory. Instead, complement is activated to the membrane attack complex (C5b-9), which inserts into the podocyte, injures its cytoskeleton and slit diaphragm, and causes heavy, nonselective proteinuria. Light microscopy shows uniformly thickened capillary walls without increased cellularity. The podocyte lays down new basement membrane between the deposits, which a silver stain shows as spikes, and the matrix later covers them (the spike and dome pattern). Immunofluorescence shows granular IgG and C3 along capillary walls, and electron microscopy shows the subepithelial deposits with effaced foot processes.

About a quarter of cases are secondary, with the deposits formed by other antigens. Causes include SLE (class V lupus nephritis), hepatitis B, solid tumors such as carcinomas of the lung, colon, and breast, and drugs including NSAIDs, penicillamine, and gold. Serum anti-PLA2R is usually negative in secondary disease, which helps separate the two groups. Membranous nephropathy carries the highest risk of renal vein thrombosis among the nephrotic diseases. Its course is variable: some patients remit, some have persistent proteinuria, and some progress to renal failure.

blocks.text: Amyloid is protein misfolded into a cross beta-pleated sheet that polymerizes into insoluble, nonbranching fibrils. The fibrils resist proteolysis and accumulate in the extracellular space. In the kidney they deposit first in the mesangium and along capillary walls and arterioles. Expanding deposits replace the normal matrix of the filter and separate the podocytes from the basement membrane, so the barrier fails and nephrotic-range proteinuria follows, usually with little hematuria. As deposits enlarge, capillary lumens are obliterated, glomeruli become acellular masses, and GFR falls. The kidneys are often normal or enlarged in size because the deposits add bulk.

Two forms dominate. AL amyloid is made of immunoglobulin light chains, more often lambda than kappa, produced by a clonal plasma cell population. It occurs in primary amyloidosis and in a minority of patients with multiple myeloma, and serum or urine immunofixation detects the monoclonal protein. AA amyloid is made from serum amyloid A, an acute phase protein that the liver produces under the influence of IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha. Chronic inflammation keeps serum amyloid A high, so AA amyloid follows rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease (especially Crohn disease), chronic osteomyelitis, tuberculosis, bronchiectasis, and familial Mediterranean fever.

The beta-pleated structure explains the stain. Congo red dye molecules align along the regular fibrils, so deposits appear salmon pink to red under ordinary light and show apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Electron microscopy shows randomly arranged nonbranching fibrils about 8 to 10 nm in diameter. Biopsy of abdominal fat or rectal mucosa can confirm systemic amyloidosis without a kidney biopsy.

blocks.text: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is an abrupt fall in GFR over hours to days, defined by consensus criteria as a rise in serum creatinine of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, a rise to 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg per hour for 6 hours. Reference values are about 0.6 to 1.2 mg/dL for creatinine and 7 to 20 mg/dL for BUN. Causes are grouped by where the problem lies.

Prerenal AKI is reduced renal perfusion, from hypovolemia, heart failure, sepsis with vasodilation, or cirrhosis, with kidneys that are structurally intact. The kidney responds appropriately: angiotensin II, aldosterone, and ADH drive avid sodium and water reabsorption, so urine sodium is low, FENa is under 1 percent, and urine osmolality is high (over about 500 mOsm/kg). Slow tubular flow and ADH-stimulated urea transport in the medullary collecting duct increase urea reabsorption, while creatinine is not reabsorbed, so the BUN to creatinine ratio exceeds 20. A diuretic given before sampling raises FENa despite low perfusion; fractional excretion of urea, under about 35 percent in prerenal states, is less affected.

Intrinsic AKI is damage to the kidney itself. The most common form is acute tubular necrosis, from prolonged ischemia or toxins such as aminoglycosides, radiocontrast, myoglobin, and ethylene glycol. Injured tubular cells cannot reabsorb sodium or concentrate the urine, so FENa exceeds 2 percent, urine osmolality approaches that of plasma (under about 350 mOsm/kg), and the BUN to creatinine ratio stays near the normal 10 to 15. Sloughed cells form muddy brown casts and obstruct tubules, and backleak of filtrate through the denuded epithelium further lowers effective GFR. Glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis, and vascular disease are other intrinsic causes.

Postrenal AKI is obstruction of urine outflow, such as prostatic enlargement, bilateral ureteral stones, or tumor. Back pressure in Bowman space opposes filtration, but total GFR falls enough to cause AKI only when both kidneys, or a single functioning kidney, are blocked. Imaging shows hydronephrosis. Early indices can resemble prerenal disease, but prolonged obstruction damages tubules and FENa rises.

blocks.title: Urinary indices in acute kidney injury
rows: Under 1 percent early, over 2 percent later
blocks.caption: Prerenal indices show intact tubules conserving sodium and water; ATN indices show tubules that can do neither.

blocks.title: Calculating FENa
blocks.text: A man with vomiting has plasma Na 140 mEq/L, plasma creatinine 2.0 mg/dL, BUN 50 mg/dL, urine Na 10 mEq/L, and urine creatinine 100 mg/dL. FENa equals (urine Na times plasma creatinine) divided by (plasma Na times urine creatinine), times 100: (10 times 2.0) divided by (140 times 100) is 20 divided by 14,000, or about 0.14 percent. The BUN to creatinine ratio is 25. Both indices show tubules conserving sodium and urea, so this is prerenal AKI from volume loss. If the same patient later had FENa of 3 percent, a ratio of 12, and muddy brown casts, prolonged hypoperfusion would have progressed to acute tubular necrosis.

blocks.predict: A patient in prerenal AKI received a loop diuretic an hour before the urine sample. What happens to FENa, and why?
blocks.explain: Loop diuretics block sodium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb, so FENa rises above 1 percent even though the tubules are healthy and perfusion is low. The fractional excretion of urea, which is less affected by these diuretics, is more reliable; a value under about 35 percent suggests prerenal disease.

blocks.text: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a GFR below 60 mL/min per 1.73 m2, or markers of kidney damage such as albuminuria, persisting for more than 3 months. Diabetes is the leading cause and hypertension the second; glomerulonephritis, polycystic kidney disease, and chronic tubulointerstitial disease follow. Hypertension damages the kidney through hyaline arteriolosclerosis that narrows afferent arterioles and causes ischemic glomerulosclerosis (benign nephrosclerosis). Whatever the cause, nephron loss leads the survivors to hyperfilter, which drives further sclerosis. Most chronically damaged kidneys are small and scarred, with waxy casts in the sediment, while diabetes, amyloidosis, polycystic disease, and HIV-associated nephropathy keep the kidneys normal or large.

Uremia results from retained urea and other nitrogenous solutes, together with the loss of the kidney's endocrine and regulatory functions. Uremic toxins cause fibrinous pericarditis and encephalopathy, which ranges from poor concentration to asterixis, seizures, and coma. They also impair platelet adhesion and aggregation, in part by disrupting von Willebrand factor binding, so bleeding time is prolonged while the platelet count, PT, and PTT are normal. Anorexia, nausea, pruritus, and peripheral neuropathy are common.

Electrolyte disorders follow the failure of excretion. Potassium is secreted by the distal nephron, and when GFR falls very low the remaining nephrons cannot excrete the daily load, so serum potassium rises above the normal range of about 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L; acidosis adds to this by shifting potassium out of cells. Fewer nephrons produce less ammonia, so acid excretion falls, causing a normal anion gap acidosis at first and a high anion gap acidosis later as sulfate, phosphate, and urate are retained. Inability to excrete sodium causes volume overload, edema, and hypertension, and the hypertension is worsened by renin release from ischemic nephrons. Anemia is normocytic and results mainly from erythropoietin deficiency, because the peritubular interstitial cells that produce it are lost to fibrosis.

blocks.title: Renal osteodystrophy and secondary hyperparathyroidism
steps: Falling GFR retains phosphate
FGF23 rises and inhibits 1-alpha-hydroxylase
Loss of renal mass further lowers calcitriol
Less intestinal calcium absorption; serum calcium falls
Low calcium, high phosphate, and low calcitriol stimulate PTH
Secondary hyperparathyroidism increases bone resorption
Osteitis fibrosa cystica, osteomalacia, vascular calcification
blocks.caption: Phosphate retention and calcitriol deficiency together drive parathyroid hyperplasia and the bone and mineral disorder of CKD.

blocks.title: Consequences of chronic kidney disease
rows: Uremic platelet dysfunction; normal count, prolonged bleeding time
Too few nephrons to secrete potassium; acidosis shifts potassium out of cells
Less ammonia production; retained sulfate and phosphate
Sodium retention plus renin from ischemic nephrons
Phosphate retention, low calcitriol, secondary hyperparathyroidism
blocks.caption: Each consequence reflects a lost excretory, regulatory, or endocrine function of the kidney.

integration.text: Glomerular disease is applied immunology on a known anatomy. The filter has three layers, and the location of injury on that structure predicts the clinical syndrome: mesangial and subendothelial deposits face the blood, recruit leukocytes, and cause nephritic disease, while subepithelial deposits and pure podocyte injury cause nephrotic disease. Complement links the immunology to the laboratory: classical pathway activation (lupus, immune complex MPGN) lowers C3 and C4, alternative pathway activation (PSGN, dense deposit disease) lowers C3 alone, and local mesangial activation (IgA nephropathy) leaves both normal. Microbiology supplies many of the antigens, including streptococcal proteins, hepatitis B and C, and HIV, and biochemistry explains diabetic glycation and amyloid fibril structure.

Physiology carries these lesions to renal failure. Lost filtering surface lowers GFR, intact or failing tubules determine the urinary indices in AKI, and surviving nephrons hyperfilter until they too scar, which is why many different diseases converge on the same CKD picture. These rules have limits. Many diseases cross the nephritic and nephrotic boundary, numerical cutoffs for FENa, urine osmolality, and the BUN to creatinine ratio are guides that diuretics, contrast, and myoglobin can distort, and the definitive diagnosis of most glomerular diseases still requires biopsy with all three methods of microscopy.

summary: Nephritic syndrome is inflammation with hematuria, RBC casts, low GFR, hypertension, and proteinuria under 3.5 g/day; nephrotic syndrome is barrier failure with proteinuria over 3.5 g/day, low albumin, edema, hyperlipidemia, and lipiduria.
Mesangial and subendothelial deposits recruit leukocytes and cause nephritic disease; subepithelial deposits and podocyte injury cause nephrotic disease.
A cast proves its contents came from the tubule: RBC casts mean glomerulonephritis, WBC casts interstitial inflammation, muddy brown casts ATN, fatty casts nephrotic syndrome, and waxy casts CKD.
PSGN appears weeks after infection with low C3 and subepithelial humps; IgA nephropathy appears within days with normal C3 and mesangial IgA.
RPGN is defined by crescents; immunofluorescence divides it into linear anti-GBM, granular immune complex, and pauci-immune ANCA types.
Class IV lupus nephritis has subendothelial wire loops and is nephritic; class V is membranous and nephrotic; low C3 and C4 with rising anti-dsDNA signal activity.
MPGN shows tram-track GBM duplication; immune complex MPGN links to hepatitis C and B, and dense deposit disease links to C3 nephritic factor with very low C3.
Diabetic nephropathy combines hyperfiltration, glycation, and efferent hyaline arteriolosclerosis, progressing from albuminuria to Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules and renal failure.

MCD is selective albuminuria with normal light microscopy and steroid response; FSGS is podocyte loss with scarring and poor response; membranous nephropathy is anti-PLA2R subepithelial disease; amyloid shows apple-green birefringence.

Prerenal AKI conserves sodium (FENa under 1 percent, BUN to creatinine over 20); ATN cannot (FENa over 2 percent); CKD causes uremia, hyperkalemia, acidosis, volume overload, anemia, and renal osteodystrophy.

verify: Latent periods for PSGN (about 1 to 3 weeks after pharyngitis, 3 to 6 weeks after impetigo) and the time for C3 to normalize (about 6 to 8 weeks) vary slightly between sources.
Whether FSGS or membranous nephropathy is the most common cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in adults differs by population and source; confirm the answer NABNE expects.

Thresholds for AKI indices vary: FENa under 1 percent and over 2 percent, urine osmolality over 500 and under 350 mOsm/kg, urine sodium under 20 and over 40 mEq/L, and a BUN to creatinine ratio over 20 (some sources use 15 to 20); fractional excretion of urea under 35 percent is a commonly cited cutoff.
KDIGO terms (moderately increased albuminuria, 30 to 300 mg/day) have replaced microalbuminuria in current guidelines; confirm which term NABNE uses.
MPGN is now classified by immunofluorescence into immune complex MPGN and C3 glomerulopathy; confirm whether NABNE still uses types I, II, and III.
The nephrotic albumin cutoff is given as below 3.0 g/dL in some sources and below 2.5 g/dL in others.
The proportion of IgA nephropathy patients reaching end-stage kidney disease (often quoted as about 20 to 40 percent over 20 years) is stated here only as a minority over about two decades.
Anti-nephrin antibodies in minimal change disease are a recent finding and are mentioned only as reported in some patients.
